Neonates of the pygmy slow loris emerge with a remarkably small body mass, with field measurements indicating a birth weight of just 21 grams [Wwb = 21 grams]. This altricial newborn is entirely dependent on its mother for thermoregulation and nutrition during the initial weeks of life, clinging to her ventral fur almost continuously. The progression from this dependent state to nutritional independence is marked by the process of weaning, which, under the stable thermal conditions of the captive environment maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], occurs at approximately 133 days after birth [tx = approximately 133 days after birth]. This protracted period of maternal investment is characteristic of the species' slow life-history strategy, allowing the offspring to develop essential motor skills and begin sampling solid foods such as gum and insects before fully transitioning away from milk. The weaning age observed in this species is notably longer than that of many similarly sized lemuriforms, highlighting the energetic demands placed on the lactating female. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a prolonged phase of somatic growth and behavioral maturation before reaching reproductive competence.

Sexual maturity in the pygmy slow loris is not attained quickly, reflecting the species' overall slow pace of life. Detailed observations from a captive breeding colony, maintained at a consistent ambient temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], revealed that puberty is reached at 273 days after birth [tp = 273 days after birth]. This delay in reproductive activation allows the growing individual to allocate significant resources toward reaching a more substantial body size before the onset of gonadal activity. The timing of this milestone is critical for understanding the species' reproductive potential, as females must achieve a certain physical threshold to support the energetic costs of gestation and subsequent lactation. The 273-day period (273 days after birth) [tp = 273 days after birth] is a substantial portion of the animal's total lifespan, indicating that a considerable fraction of life is spent in a pre-reproductive, somatic growth phase at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This contrasts sharply with the accelerated maturation schedules seen in many small-bodied prosimians from less seasonal or more unpredictable environments.

The gestation period of the pygmy slow loris reflects its phylogenetic position among the strepsirrhines, lasting approximately 188 days [tg = approximately 188 days] under the controlled thermoneutral conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This extended pregnancy, which is long for a mammal of its adult body size, results in the birth of a single, well-developed offspring that is already furred and has its eyes open, though it remains incapable of independent locomotion for several weeks. The physiological demands of this prolonged gestation place a considerable metabolic burden on the female, who must increase her caloric intake substantially to support foetal growth and placental function. The duration of 188 days [tg = 188 days] is consistent with the pattern observed in other Nycticebus species and is thought to be linked to their relatively low basal metabolic rates and arboreal, energy-conserving lifestyle at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This investment in a long gestation is a key component of the species' life-history strategy, prioritizing offspring quality at birth over high fecundity, which is instead reflected in a very low maximum reproductive rate.

The pygmy slow loris is characterized by an exceptionally low maximum reproductive rate, a direct consequence of its slow life-history and extended periods of parental investment. Under optimal captive conditions at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females are capable of producing a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], and the inter-birth interval is such that they typically raise only one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This combination of a single offspring per event and a low frequency of reproductive events results in a very modest annual output, limiting the species' capacity for rapid population growth. The ultimate wet weight of adults provides context for this reproductive strategy; a female can attain a maximum body mass of 419 grams [Wwi = 419 grams], a size that demands considerable energy for maintenance and gestation. This low reproductive output makes the species particularly vulnerable to population declines from habitat loss or poaching, as compensatory recruitment is severely constrained by their biology. The trade-off between investing heavily in a single, high-quality offspring and producing multiple young is starkly resolved in favor of the former.

Longevity records from both captive and wild populations indicate that the pygmy slow loris can achieve a maximum lifespan of approximately 19.4 years [am = approximately 19.4 years] when maintained at a stable body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, which translates to about 7,081 days, is exceptionally long for a mammal weighing less than half a kilogram, standing in stark contrast to the short lifespans typical of many small-bodied primates. The species' ultimate adult body mass of 419 grams [Wwi = 419 grams] is achieved gradually over several years, a slow growth trajectory that is inextricably linked to its low metabolic rate and extended developmental periods. This extended lifespan allows for repeated reproductive opportunities across many years, partially offsetting the extremely low annual fecundity. From a comparative perspective, the slow loris exemplifies the extreme end of the slow-fast life-history continuum among primates, investing heavily in somatic durability and longevity at the cost of high reproductive output. This strategy is well-suited to the relatively stable, low-mortality environments of the Southeast Asian forests they inhabit.
